title: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage

guidelineVersions: Resuscitation Council UK, Special Circumstances Guidelines 2021 (published May 2021)
Royal College of Surgeons of England, National Prospective Tonsillectomy Audit: Final Report (2005)

related.why: The larynx and emergency front-of-neck airway, relevant if the airway is compromised by ongoing bleeding

brief.scenario: Mr Jamie Underwood, 24, presents with fresh bleeding six days after tonsillectomy and reports coughing up blood for the last hour.
brief.task: Manage suspected post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage as the examiner questions your priorities.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A tonsil bed bleed is an airway emergency until proven otherwise, not a routine ENT referral.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Discharging or reassuring him once visible bleeding has stopped.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd treat this as a potentially life-threatening airway and haemorrhage emergency and call for senior ENT and anaesthetic help now."

flow: Sit forward, protect the airway, ABCDE
Prepare for theatre, not oral intake
Do not discharge on bleeding stopping

grid.label: Treat as an airway/haemorrhage emergency (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats him as a minor bleed and completes routine triage before senior review.
grid.pass: Recognises post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage as a potentially life-threatening airway and haemorrhage emergency; calls ENT senior and anaesthetic/resuscitation support early.
grid.high: Requests simultaneous ENT and anaesthetic attendance rather than sequential referral, anticipating a difficult airway.

grid.label: Immediate positioning and ABCDE
grid.fail: Lies him flat to examine the throat, or leaves him unmonitored while arranging tests.
grid.pass: Sits him forward if conscious and bleeding, protects the airway, and runs ABCDE with attention to haemodynamic status.
grid.high: Anticipates that swallowed blood can mask the true extent of haemorrhage, so treats on clinical trajectory, not just visible loss.

grid.label: Avoid instrumenting the fossa
grid.fail: Repeatedly examines or manipulates the tonsillar fossa with instruments.
grid.pass: Avoids blind manipulation of the tonsillar fossae; leaves definitive assessment to ENT.
grid.high: Explains that repeated examination can provoke further bleeding and rapid airway deterioration.

grid.label: Prepare for theatre, not oral intake
grid.fail: Gives oral fluids or food despite likely need for theatre.
grid.pass: Keeps him nil by mouth, obtains IV access and blood tests/crossmatch as indicated, anticipating operative management.
grid.high: Flags him early to theatre and anaesthetics so a return to theatre isn't delayed by avoidable preparation steps.

grid.label: Does not discharge on bleeding stopping (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Discharges or reassures the patient because the visible bleeding has stopped.
grid.pass: Arranges urgent ENT assessment regardless of whether bleeding has stopped, because it can recur.
grid.high: Explains that bleeds serious enough to need hospital care can recur even after apparently settling, so admits for observation rather than discharging.

grid.label: Definitive management
grid.fail: Plans conservative management alone for ongoing or significant bleeding.
grid.pass: Recognises that recurrent or significant bleeding may need examination under anaesthesia and surgical haemostasis.
grid.high: Discusses with ENT the choice between EUA/haemostasis and conservative measures based on trajectory and severity, and ensures major haemorrhage support is available if bleeding is significant.

grid.label: Communicates the plan
grid.fail: Does not explain to Jamie why he needs to stay or proceed to theatre.
grid.pass: Explains clearly why he needs to stay for observation or theatre despite the bleeding stopping, and documents the discussion.
grid.high: Checks his understanding and directly addresses his concerns about repeat bleeding or theatre, using plain language.

failures.move: Treating a post-tonsillectomy bleed as routine triage rather than an emergency.
failures.consequence: Delays senior ENT and anaesthetic input while the airway and haemorrhage risk are evolving.

failures.move: Repeatedly examining the fossa with instruments.
failures.consequence: Can provoke further bleeding and rapid airway compromise.

failures.move: Discharging once visible bleeding has stopped.
failures.consequence: Misses a recurrence that can be life-threatening at home.

failures.move: Giving oral fluids or food while awaiting ENT review.
failures.consequence: Delays safe anaesthesia if he needs theatre.

recovery.when: Asked why not discharge if it's stopped
recovery.line: Because it can recur, and recurrence after apparent settling happens often enough that he needs urgent ENT assessment first.

recovery.when: Pushed to examine the throat again
recovery.line: I'd rather not repeat that myself — it risks provoking more bleeding; I'll let ENT assess it properly.

knowledge.fact: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage is a potentially life-threatening airway and haemorrhage emergency needing urgent senior ENT and anaesthetic involvement.
Swallowed blood can obscure the true amount of haemorrhage.
About 3% of patients have a secondary haemorrhage needing hospital readmission; of 1,309 readmissions overall, 13% returned to theatre and 4% needed transfusion.
Recurrent or significant bleeding may need examination under anaesthesia and surgical haemostasis.

recall.think: Airway compromise from ongoing or recurrent haemorrhage.
recall.say: "This is a potential airway/haemorrhage emergency — ENT and anaesthetics now."
do: IV access, bloods/crossmatch, nil by mouth
Urgent ENT assessment, even if bleeding has stopped

numbers.value: ~3% secondary haemorrhage rate; of 1,309 readmissions overall, 13% returned to theatre
numbers.meaning: post-tonsillectomy bleeding is not rare and can need surgical haemostasis

recall.trap: Assuming the bleeding has truly stopped because it isn't visible right now.
recall.finish: Urgent ENT review; examination under anaesthesia and haemostasis if bleeding is recurrent or significant.

partner.opening: Mr Jamie Underwood, 24, presents with fresh bleeding six days after tonsillectomy. What do you do first?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for observations or examines
reveals.finding: HR 118, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 97% on air, alert. Active fresh bleeding visible from the left tonsillar fossa. Swallowing frequently.

reveals.trigger: Candidate positions him or asks about ongoing bleeding
reveals.finding: Sitting forward, the visible bleeding appears to slow but he continues swallowing; some fresh blood is still seen at the back of the throat.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for bloods and group and save
reveals.finding: Hb 128 g/L (baseline 142 last week). Group and save and crossmatch of 2 units requested.
Visible bleeding has stopped; he says he feels less anxious now.

push.question: Why not just observe him on the ward?
push.expect: This is a potential airway/haemorrhage emergency needing urgent senior ENT and anaesthetic input, not routine observation.

push.question: Can you have a look in his throat to check?
push.expect: Avoids blind instrumentation of the fossa; leaves formal assessment to ENT.

push.question: He wants a drink, is that OK?
push.expect: No — nil by mouth, IV access and crossmatch, anticipating theatre.

push.question: The bleeding's stopped now, can he go home?
push.expect: No — urgent ENT assessment regardless, because it can recur.

curveballs.prompt: He becomes acutely more breathless and the bleeding restarts heavily.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Call for immediate senior anaesthetic and ENT help, sit him forward, give high-flow oxygen, and prepare for a difficult airway and probable emergency theatre.

curveballs.prompt: ENT is currently in theatre with another patient.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Escalate to the on-call consultant and anaesthetics directly given the airway risk; don't wait passively.

curveballs.prompt: He asks to just go home because he's scared of surgery.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain the risk of recurrent, potentially life-threatening bleeding and why urgent assessment is needed, and address his fear directly.

curveballs.prompt: A nurse asks if she can offer him some water since he seems settled.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — keep him nil by mouth until ENT has assessed him and a plan for theatre is excluded.
